1.note: Isaiah is using the word **Woe** to express a strong feeling of warning and judgment. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Isaiah was feeling, or you could say what made him sorrowful. Alternate translation: [Judgment will come upon]

These two phrases **the ones decreeing decrees of iniquity** and **the writers, they write oppression** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [those who make unjust decrees, they write oppressive laws]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the verb **decree** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [the ones who make such terrible decrees of]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wicked things]

2.note: Here, **to** marks **turn aside the needy ones from judgment and to rob the justice of the poor of my people** as the goal or purpose of “decreeing decrees of iniquity” in the previous verse. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [for turning aside]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment** you could express the same idea in other ways. Alternate translation: [fair rulings]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the rights]

3.q: וּ⁠מַֽה־תַּעֲשׂוּ֙ לְ⁠י֣וֹם פְּקֻדָּ֔ה וּ⁠לְ⁠שׁוֹאָ֖ה מִ⁠מֶּרְחָ֣ק תָּב֑וֹא
3.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that they will be completely helpless. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And you will be completely helpless on the day of visitation when the desolation comes from afar.]

Isaiah is using **the day of visitation** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the time when God comes to punish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when God comes to punish you]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **visitation** and **desolation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [his punishing you and about destruction of your land by enemies]

3.q: עַל־מִי֙ תָּנ֣וּסוּ לְ⁠עֶזְרָ֔ה וְ⁠אָ֥נָה תַעַזְב֖וּ כְּבוֹדְ⁠כֶֽם
3.note: Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that there is no one who can help them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You will have no one to whom you can flee for help and nowhere to leave your glory.]

4.note: The pronoun **One** refers to each of the unjust leaders of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Each unjust leader will only bow down with the prisoner]

The phrase **In all of this** introduces a concessive statement, indicating that despite the preceding judgment, what follows is still true. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Despite all of this]
Here, **his nose** represents Yahweh’s anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his anger has not turned back]
The pronoun **his** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s nose has not turned back, and Yahweh’s hand {is} still stretched out]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative phrase **turned back**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [his nose still burns]
Here, **his hand** represents Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his arm is still]

5.note: Yahweh is using the word **Woe** to express warning about his strong feeling of anger and intention to deliver judgment against Assyria. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what Yahweh was feeling, or you could say what made him angry. Alternate translation: [It will be terrible for Assyria]
Here, **my nose** represents Yahweh’s anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the rod of my anger]

Yahweh is speaking as if Assyria were **the rod** that he uses to punish other nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the means by which I punish nations]
The pronoun **their** refers to the Assyrians. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the staff in the hand of the Assyrians, it is my fury]

6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the mud of the streets** is trampled underfoot, so the conquered nation will be trampled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and to trample them underfoot just as mud in the streets is trampled]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verbs **spoil** and **plunder** in order to intensify his expression of the ideas that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [to completely despoil and to utterly plunder]

7.note: Isaiah uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between Yahweh’s purpose for Assyria and Assyria’s own intentions. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However, he]

The word **heart** represents where the king of Assyria’s thoughts and intentions exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he does not think this way]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

Isaiah is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [in great number]

8.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form to boast that his commanders are as powerful as kings. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [All my commanders are kings.]

9.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form to assert that Calno fell to him just as Carchemish did. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Calno fell just as Carchemish fell]

9.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֥א כְּ⁠כַרְכְּמִ֖ישׁ כַּלְנ֑וֹ אִם־לֹ֤א כְ⁠אַרְפַּד֙ חֲמָ֔ת אִם־לֹ֥א כְ⁠דַמֶּ֖שֶׂק שֹׁמְרֽוֹן
9.note: The words **Calno**, **Carchemish**, **Hamath**, **Arpad**, **Samaria**, and **Damascus** are the names of cities.

The king of Assyria is using the question form to assert that Hamath fell to him just as Arpad did. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Hamath fell just as Arpad fell.]

The Assyrian king is not using the term **Or** to ask listeners to say whether the situation described in this question is the actual one, as opposed to the situation described in the preceding question. He is using the term to introduce this question as further description of what the preceding question describes. Your language may have a connecting word that would show how this question relates to the one before it. In some languages, it may be clearer not to use a connecting word. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

The king of Assyria is using the question form to assert that Samaria fell to him just as Damascus did. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Samaria fell just as Damascus fell.]
See how you translated the term **Or** in the previous instance in this verse. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

10.q: כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁר֙ מָצְאָ֣ה יָדִ֔⁠י לְ⁠מַמְלְכֹ֖ת הָ⁠אֱלִ֑יל וּ⁠פְסִ֣ילֵי⁠הֶ֔ם מִ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִַ֖ם וּ⁠מִ⁠שֹּׁמְרֽוֹן
10.note: The king of Assyria is using **As my hand has found kingdoms of the idol, and their images were more than Jerusalem and than Samaria** to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for the claim he will make in the next verse. Connect this clause to the story in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [Since my hand had found kingdoms of the idol, and their images were more than Jerusalem and than Samaria,]

Here, **my hand** represents the king of Assyria’s power and military capability. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my power has conquered]

11.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֗א כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשִׂ֛יתִי לְ⁠שֹׁמְר֖וֹן וְ⁠לֶ⁠אֱלִילֶ֑י⁠הָ כֵּ֛ן אֶעֱשֶׂ֥ה לִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם וְ⁠לַ⁠עֲצַבֶּֽי⁠הָ
11.note: The king of Assyria is using the question form to assert with confidence that he will conquer Jerusalem just as he conquered Samaria. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [as I have done to Samaria and to its idols, I will certainly do the same to Jerusalem and to its idols!]

12.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֗ה כִּֽי־יְבַצַּ֤ע אֲדֹנָ⁠י֙ אֶת־כָּל־מַֽעֲשֵׂ֔⁠הוּ בְּ⁠הַ֥ר צִיּ֖וֹן וּ⁠בִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם אֶפְקֹ֗ד עַל־פְּרִי־גֹ֨דֶל֙ לְבַ֣ב מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁ֔וּר וְ⁠עַל־תִּפְאֶ֖רֶת ר֥וּם עֵינָֽי⁠ו
12.note: The punishment of Assyria will not happen until after the Lord has finished his work on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [And it will happen, after the Lord has finished all of his work on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, I will visit against the fruit of the greatness of heart of the king of Assyria and against the splendor of the height of his eyes.]

Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **And it will happen** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, who is now speaking directly. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, the Lord, will visit against]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **fruit** that is produced by **the greatness of heart of the king of Assyria**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the arrogant pride of the king of Assyria has produced]

Isaiah is speaking as if the king of Assyria’s pride were a tree producing **fruit**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the results of]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [very great]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **splendor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and against the glorious height of his eyes]

Here, **the height of his eyes** represents the king of Assyria’s arrogance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his haughty eyes]

13.note: The king of Assyria is using the possessive expression **the strength of my hand** to say that his **hand**, that is, his power, is characterized by **strength**. By using the terms hand (power) and strength together, he is intensifying their meaning. If a speaker of your language would not use a possessive form for this purpose, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For by my great power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [and because think wisely]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a mighty one** brings down those in power, so the king of Assyria claims to have brought down the rulers of the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as a powerful warrior brings down rulers, so I have brought down those who sit on thrones]

The king of Assyria is saying **the sitters** to represent kings who sit on thrones to rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [kings who were ruling]

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as eggs in **a nest** can be easily taken, so the king of Assyria found the wealth of the nations easy to seize. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And my hand has found, as easily as taking from a nest, the wealth of the peoples]

Here, **my hand** represents the king of Assyria’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And my power has found]

The point of this comparison is that just as **one gathers abandoned eggs** without resistance, so the king of Assyria gathered the wealth of the nations without opposition. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and just as one gathers eggs from an abandoned nest without any resistance]

The pronoun **I** refers to the king of Assyria, who states it emphatically to stress that he himself accomplished this. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, the king of Assyria, have gathered]

The king of Assyria says **all of the earth** as an exaggeration to emphasize how extensively he has conquered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [I myself have gathered the whole earth]

14.q: וְ⁠לֹ֤א הָיָה֙ נֹדֵ֣ד כָּנָ֔ף וּ⁠פֹצֶ֥ה פֶ֖ה וּ⁠מְצַפְצֵֽף
14.note: The king of Assyria is speaking as if the conquered peoples were helpless **birds** that could not even flutter a wing or chirp to resist him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and no one resisted or even cried out in protest]

15.q: הֲ⁠יִתְפָּאֵר֙ הַ⁠גַּרְזֶ֔ן עַ֖ל הַ⁠חֹצֵ֣ב בּ֑⁠וֹ אִם־יִתְגַּדֵּ֤ל הַ⁠מַּשּׂוֹר֙ עַל־מְנִיפ֔⁠וֹ
15.note: Isaiah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The axe certainly does not exalt itself against the one hewing with it! The saw certainly does not magnify itself against the one moving it!]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **axe** or **saw**. He means those tools in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [an axe … a saw]
See how you translated the term “Or” in 10:9.

15.q: כְּ⁠הָנִ֥יף שֵׁ֨בֶט֙ וְ⁠אֶת־מְרִימָ֔י⁠ו כְּ⁠הָרִ֥ים מַטֶּ֖ה לֹא־עֵֽץ
15.note: Yahweh is using the expression **As if** in each instance to introduce a possibility that is certainly not the case. Your language may have its own way of indicating that a statement is certainly not true. Alternate translation: [A rod certainly does not wield its lifter! A club certainly does not lift what is not wood!]

16.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [For this reason]

Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s punishment were **leanness** sent among the Assyrians, who are described as **fat ones**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will cause his well-fed ones to waste away]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **leanness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a wasting disease]

Here, **his glory** represents the king of Assyria’s splendid possessions and wealth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and among his splendid possessions]
The pronoun **his** refers to the king of Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [leanness among the fat ones of Assyria, and among Assyria’s glory]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the burning of a fire** consumes everything it touches, so Yahweh’s judgment will consume the Assyrians. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will kindle a fire that will burn and consume] or [he will start a conflagration]

17.note: Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh, **the light of Israel**, would literally become **a fire** that would burn and consume the Assyrians. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who gives light to Israel, will be as destructive as a fire]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and his Holy One will become a flame]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh, **his Holy One**, were a **flame** that would burn and consume. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his Holy One will act like a burning flame]

In connection to the **thorn** and the **briar**, the pronoun **his** refers to Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and it will burn and consume Assyria’s thorn and Assyria’s briar]

Isaiah is speaking as if the Assyrians were worthless weeds, **his thorn and his briar**, that Yahweh would burn up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his enemies]

These two phrases **his thorn** and **his briar** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [his thorny briars]

18.note: Isaiah is speaking as if the Assyrian nation had a **forest** and **agricultural land** that Yahweh would destroy. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the glory of his productive land]

Isaiah is referring to all of the Assyrian empire by naming two extremes, **soul** and **flesh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of it]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will consume]

The point of this comparison is that just as **one wasting away** grows weak and diminished, so the Assyrian empire will be weakened and diminished. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and just as one wasting away grows weak and diminishes, so Assyria will be weakened and diminished]

19.note: Isaiah exaggerates when he says **a child may write them** to emphasize how few Assyrian trees will remain. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [a number so small that even a child could count them]

It might seem that the expression **a number that a child may write them** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [a number that a child may write]

20.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **And it will happen on that day** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of an **escape**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people who escaped] or [those who survived]

Here, **the house of Jacob** means all the people descended from Jacob. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Jacob]

It might seem that saying both **add** and **again** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you could use just one of these terms in your translation. Alternate translation: [will not again support itself]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [truly]

22.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the sand of the sea** is innumerable, so the people of Israel are very numerous. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [For though your people, Israel, are very numerous]

The expression **has been decreed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has decreed destruction]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Destruction**, you could express the same idea in other ways. Alternate translation: [Destroying them]
If your language does not use an abstract nouns for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in other ways. Alternate translation: [rightful actions]

23.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

The expression **a decreed one** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [one that he has decreed]

24.note: The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [For this reason]
The phrase **thus says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies** introduces a direct quotation of what Yahweh says. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

The phrase translated as **May you not be afraid** is an imperative, but it communicates encouragement rather than a direct command. If the imperative does not communicate this for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates encouragement. Alternate translation: [You do not need to be afraid]

Isaiah is speaking as if the Assyrian oppression consisted of being struck with **the rod** and having a **staff** lifted against the people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will oppress you just as Egypt oppressed your ancestors]
The pronoun **He** refers to the king of Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The king of Assyria will strike you, my people,]

Isaiah is using **in the way of Egypt** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the same manner as the Egyptians treated you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the Egyptians did to you]

25.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [For yet a little while]

These two phrases **a little** and **a trifle** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [a very short time]

Here, **my nose** represents Yahweh’s anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my anger will result in their destruction]
The pronoun **their** refers to the Assyrians. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will result in the destruction of the Assyrians]

26.note: The word **Then** indicates that this event happens after Yahweh’s fury against his own people has been completed. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [After that, Yahweh of Armies will awaken]

Isaiah is speaking of **a whip** as if it were a living thing that Yahweh could **awaken**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then Yahweh of Armies will wield a whip against him]

Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s punishment were **a whip** that he would use against the Assyrians. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then Yahweh of Armies will rise up to punish him]
The pronoun **him** refers to leader or king who stands for the entire nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Assyrians]

The point of this comparison is that just as Yahweh struck **Midian at the rock of Oreb** and gave Israel a decisive victory, so Yahweh will defeat the Assyrians. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as Yahweh struck the Midianites at the rock of Oreb]
The word **Oreb** is the name of a place.
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:24. Alternate translation: [as he did when he freed your ancestors from Egypt]

27.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 10:20.

27.q: יָס֤וּר סֻבֳּל⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל שִׁכְמֶ֔⁠ךָ וְ⁠עֻלּ֖⁠וֹ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל צַוָּארֶ֑⁠ךָ
27.note: Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [his burden will turn away from upon your shoulder, and his yoke will turn away from upon your neck,]
